deep_why: ESCOMIC ranks comic pages by scoring how well they match a query across visual appearance and story characteristics. The core insight is that this ranking improves when the weight given to each facet (like visual style or pacing) adapts based on which facets the user repeatedly engages with. This works because implicit feedback from user interactions reveals what matters in the current search intent: if a user ignores style but lingers on pace, boosting the pace facet in future rankings will pull results closer to their actual goal. By explicitly showing which facets drove each ranking decision, users can validate that the system understood them correctly, building trust. This transforms search from opaque to interpretable, letting comics fans find stories matching their mood in ways generic image-text search cannot.

WISE retrieves images and video by first converting each query modality (text about a scene, a photo of a face, a sound file) into a fixed-size numerical summary, then finding stored summaries that are closest to the query summary. This works because when summaries are built by the same process for both queries and documents, two things that humans find similar will have summaries that sit near each other in storage. Scaling to millions of images works because finding nearby summaries is fundamentally faster than comparing each query to every image pixel-by-pixel. The key is that the system lets users combine facets freely: asking for a train and filtering by metadata works because each facet (object, scene, speech, metadata) stays independent until fusion, so adding one constraint just removes non-matching results. This modular design lets the system grow to handle any combination users need.

PatentMerit scores individual patents and clusters of patents by analyzing how technologies build on and diverge from each other using citation networks and language meaning. The soundness rests on a basic truth: if many other patents cite a patent and extend its ideas in diverse directions, that patent likely unlocked something valuable. By treating patents as nodes in a network and tracing flow through citations, the system computes influence scores that reflect genuine technical momentum, not just filing volume or age. Combining network flow with topic extraction lets the system spot when a patent introduces a genuinely new technical direction versus incremental refinement. This approach surfaces real innovation signals buried in bibliographic noise, letting R&D teams focus on patents that actually shaped a field's evolution.

Visual RAG at Scale reduces retrieval cost by first pooling thousands of image patches into dozens of compact tile summaries per page, then using these summaries for fast initial candidate filtering, followed by precise reranking with full details. This cascading strategy works because at the filtering stage, a coarse summary is sufficient to reject irrelevant pages: if a tile summary doesn't resemble the query at all, the full page will not either. Only for genuinely close candidates is the precision cost of full comparison justified. Matryoshka embeddings guarantee that shorter summaries preserve ranking order for top candidates, so early filtering does not corrupt final results. The quadratic speedup comes from reducing the sheer number of numerical comparisons, trading insignificant accuracy loss for throughput gain where it matters most.

EasyRAG teaches RAG concepts through three progressively complex implementations that each extend the prior one. The pedagogy works because learners first see the simplest form—fetch external text, feed it to a language model, receive an answer—which immediately reveals the basic value proposition over models alone. Each subsequent level introduces a real trade-off: speed versus coverage, or end-to-end tuning versus computational cost. By implementing these methods side-by-side and showing how they differ mathematically, students build intuition for why each design choice matters. The framework succeeds by isolating each conceptual piece rather than presenting RAG as a monolithic black box, letting beginners understand the decision points they will face when building real systems.

Building a standardized Nepali IR benchmark creates a shared test set that lets researchers measure retrieval quality on Nepali text using agreed metrics. This is foundational because without consensus on what counts as correct, different groups will report incomparable results and cannot build incrementally on prior work. The benchmark's value is anchored in Nepali's morphological richness: words in Nepali have complex internal structure that affects matching, so retrieval methods tuned for English will fail. Including cross-lingual and code-mixed test cases matters because real Nepali speakers often mix Nepali with English, so any practical system must handle this shift. This benchmark removes the excuse that tools cannot be built for Nepali and provides the objective measuring stick needed to drive field progress.

This work systematically tests whether using a language model to expand queries or rerank results helps or hurts retrieval for Hausa and Fongbe. The core principle is straightforward: if language model quality is high, its rewrites will improve signal; if quality is low, rewritten queries will add noise. By measuring language model translation quality independently and correlating it with downstream retrieval gains, the study reveals the bottleneck: Fongbe translations are severely degraded compared to Hausa, and generated text hurts downstream tasks more often than it helps. This empirical linking of upstream quality to downstream impact lets practitioners decide whether to trust LLM interventions or stick with simpler methods for their target language. The study's real contribution is this diagnosis—showing that language-specific evaluation, not generic best practices, must guide IR deployment choices.

This paper tests whether prompting a small language model in three languages separately and combining the predictions improves query classification over English-alone. The soundness comes from the observation that different languages encode intent using different grammatical cues: Hindi may highlight relationships through suffixes, Bengali through word order, and English through vocabulary. When a model sees the same conceptual query expressed three different ways, each language highlights different subtle signals that the model can pick up. Averaging these three independent signals, weighted by confidence, creates a composite prediction that reflects evidence from multiple angles. Cross-lingual diversity drives gains more than surface variation does, proving the mechanism is linguistic depth, not just ensemble averaging. This technique succeeds because it extracts information already latent in the frozen model without requiring retraining or external services.

This work adapts language models for Text-to-SQL in Chichewa by applying efficient fine-tuning and combining it with retrieval-based prompting. The two techniques work together because efficient tuning updates a small parameter subset to improve Chichewa fluency, while retrieval provides in-context examples of successful Chichewa-to-SQL pairs. Tuning alone cannot overcome the domain gap (Chichewa was barely represented in pretraining), but tuning combined with relevant examples lets the model leverage those examples as scaffolding. The 23.4 percentage point gap between English and Chichewa execution accuracy reveals the underlying challenge: the model has learned SQL reasoning better in English-dominated data. By measuring both tuning variants and retrieval strategies separately, the paper shows that neither alone suffices, but their combination bridges the gap. This demonstrates that low-resource language adaptation requires stacking techniques, each addressing a different bottleneck.

This gap analysis surveys available agricultural information sources for Telugu-speaking farmers and finds that none meet the intersection of three criteria: Telugu language, agricultural focus, and question-answering format that accepts Rayalaseema drought contexts. The study's framing is powerful because it anchors the benchmark need in a real, underserved population facing a concrete problem: drought-vulnerable marginal farmers need practical guidance but cannot access English-language or generalist systems. A Telugu agricultural QA dataset would let researchers build and evaluate retrieval and generation models for this specific population. The roadmap matters because it shows how to construct such a dataset from existing regional sources rather than starting from zero. By documenting the gap explicitly, the work makes the business case: a benchmark fills a void that blocks equitable access for 74 million speakers.

MarathiWeb evaluates web-augmented language models by separating globally translated queries from locally native queries and measuring whether the model can retrieve and integrate relevant information from the web. The test reveals that despite high rates of web search invocation, accuracy drops sharply for local queries in Marathi, suggesting the bottleneck is not tool calling but evidence integration: the model retrieves pages but struggles to extract or synthesize relevant text. The finding that shallow retrieval (one search) outperforms deeper multi-step search is striking and constrains future system designs: the model apparently hallucinates connections between searches more than additional searches help. This benchmark's value lies in isolating integration failure from retrieval failure, exposing that language model web search still requires fundamental improvements in reading comprehension, not just tool availability. The cost-accuracy trade-off is practically important for deployment in low-resource regions with metered bandwidth.

Graph-Enhanced Sentence Retrieval improves abstractive summarization in low-resource languages by first extracting sentences that matter most, sidestepping generation hallucination entirely. The soundness is direct: extracted sentences are guaranteed to appear in source documents, making the summary faithful by construction. The method scales to low-resource languages through a mixture-of-experts design: instead of one large model, multiple small experts collaborate, each specializing in linguistic phenomena common to certain language families. Adding graph structure modeling discourse relationships lets the model score sentences not just by content but by how they connect to surrounding sentences, improving extraction coherence. With only 3.2M parameters, training completes on a single GPU and fits available budgets. This approach trades elegant end-to-end generation for faithful, compute-efficient extraction, a pragmatic compromise when truthfulness and resources matter more than stylistic polish.

This study trains a text classifier to distinguish LLM-generated answers from human-written answers on agricultural questions in Swahili. The method works because language models generate text with consistent statistical properties: longer sequences, lower word-diversity patterns, and measurable similarity to their training data all appear reliably in generated text. A logistic regression classifier learns these patterns and achieves 0.98 accuracy, proving the patterns are strong and learnable. The 0.98 accuracy signals that generated answers exhibit fingerprints of their origin. This detectability matters for IR system evaluation: when answers come from language models, knowing which ones are generated versus human-expert answers lets evaluators adjust their trust and audit output quality. In low-resource agricultural settings where misinformation spreads rapidly and farmer welfare depends on answer reliability, detectability becomes a diagnostic tool for assurance.

Tulun combines machine translation with language model post-editing, guided by user-maintained translation memories and domain glossaries, to improve technical translation for low-resource languages like Tetun and Bislama. The system works because translation memory and glossaries anchor terminology: if a specialized term appears in translation memory with its prior correct translation, fetching and using that example in the language model prompt improves consistency and accuracy. Domain granularity matters because medical terminology differs radically from general discourse; broad categories miss this specificity. The 16-22 ChrF++ point improvement comes from in-context learning: the language model corrects and contextualizes machine-translation output when shown relevant domain examples. Transparency to end-users is crucial because it lets them understand why choices were made and refine glossaries, creating a human-in-the-loop cycle. This retrieval-augmented approach succeeds where traditional machine translation alone fails on technical domains.

Morphology-Aware Retrieval for Shona addresses a fundamental linguistic challenge: Shona is a morphologically complex language where words combine stems with prefixes and suffixes that carry grammatical information. Standard English-tuned retrieval methods treat these words as atomic units and fail to recognize that two Shona sentences with different surface words may express the same meaning through morphological variation. Retrieval requires matching semantically equivalent forms, so a method must decompose words into meaningful parts or learn their relationships from training data. A large-scale benchmark dataset lets researchers train and test methods specifically on Shona morphology, measuring whether morphology-aware approaches outperform generic dense retrieval. This benchmark removes the perception that Shona is too small or obscure to work on and creates the objective yardstick needed to build inclusive tools. Equitable digital access depends on having language-specific methods where linguistic structure demands them.
